how.title: How to serve snails
how.lead: Each jar is a ready dish: 100 g of tender snail meat that takes on the flavour of its sauce. Three ways, each in 5 minutes.

ways.title: On toast
ways.text: Snails in lemon and parsley oil, warmed for 2–3 minutes, on toasted baguette rubbed with garlic. Parsley and a squeeze of lemon.

ways.title: With pasta
ways.text: Snails in green pesto or tomato sauce, sautéed for 3–4 minutes and tossed with tagliatelle or spaghetti. A spoonful of pasta water makes it silky.

ways.title: In a tartlet
ways.text: Ready-made shortcrust tartlets filled with snails in court-bouillon, garlic butter and grated cheese. 5–7 minutes at 200°C.

faq.a: A ready dish: 100 g of tender snail meat in stock, oil or sauce, 250 g per jar. The meat is already cooked and seasoned; just heat it.
Delicate, a little like mushrooms or mussels. The texture is tender and springy, and the meat takes on the flavour of its sauce: garlic, lemon, pesto.

faq.q: Are there shells in the jar?
faq.a: No. Our jars contain snail meat only, ready to eat once warmed.

faq.q: Where do the snails come from?
faq.a: From Polish snail farms. We cook them in our small, veterinary-approved kitchen in Kołomań, in the Świętokrzyskie region.
Unopened jars keep for 12 months at room temperature in a cool, dry place. Once opened, refrigerate and eat within 3 days.
Snails are molluscs, one of the allergens listed on food labels. The pesto contains walnuts and cheese, the tomato sauce contains celery. Full ingredients are listed for each jar.

kitchen.title: Our kitchen
kitchen.lead: A forgotten Polish delicacy returns to the table. Where it comes from, who cooks it and why it is worth a try.

story.title: Snails were a Polish delicacy
story.text: Our ancestors ate them. Snail recipes already appear in the first Polish cookbook, Stanisław Czerniecki’s “Compendium ferculorum” of 1682.

story.title: Poland forgot them, yet still produces them
story.text: For years Poland has farmed snails and exported them, mainly to France, while hardly eating them at home.

story.title: Lumaca brings them back to the Polish table
story.text: In a modern form: ready-made dishes from Polish-farmed snails, prepared in a small kitchen in Świętokrzyskie. Just heat and serve.

kitchen.owners_text: Lumaca is run by Grażyna Nawrocka and her husband, Tomasz Nawrocki. They started out farming snails and later turned to cooking them: today Lumaca buys snails from trusted Polish farms, and their own recipes are cooked in the kitchen in Kołomań.

facts.title: Polish farms
facts.text: Gros gris snails (Helix aspersa maxima) from Polish farms, with certificates of origin and veterinary certificates.

facts.title: A small kitchen
facts.text: Our processing kitchen in Kołomań is veterinary-approved (no. PL26040901). We cook in small batches.

facts.title: Our own recipes
facts.text: The snail meat is simmered for 120 minutes in vegetable stock with dry white wine, then finished in sauces made to our recipes.

facts.title: Tested labels and shelf life
facts.text: Labels checked by the Polish food quality inspectorate (IJHARS). Twelve months at room temperature, confirmed by SGS laboratory tests.

facts.title: A vintage
facts.text: We buy snails once a year, in autumn. Each batch is a natural vintage, as with wine: the jars now hold the 2026 vintage.
